title: Guess the Number Using Bitwise Questions I
statement:
A positive integer `n` is hidden from you, and your task is to return it.

The only way to learn about `n` is a global function `commonSetBits(num)`. It returns how many bit positions are `1` in both `n` and `num`, that is, the number of set bits in `n & num` (bitwise AND). Only ask about values `num` from `0` to `2^30 - 1`: LeetCode gives unreliable answers outside that range, and the local judge stops a solution that asks about one.

Your function is `findNumber()` and takes no arguments. Each test case is written as `[n]`: that is the hidden number the judge uses to answer `commonSetBits`, and it is never passed to you.
constraints: Every num passed to commonSetBits must satisfy 0 <= num <= 2^30 - 1
api: findNumber(): number, using the global commonSetBits(num: number): number
notes:
## Intuition

`n` fits in 30 bits, so knowing it means knowing each of those 30 bits. Asking about a number with a single `1` bit, `num = 1 << bit`, makes `n & num` either `0` or exactly that one bit, so `commonSetBits` answers `1` precisely when `n` has that bit set. Thirty such questions reveal every bit, and setting the confirmed bits rebuilds `n`. (Another way: ask about all 30 bits together, then leave out one bit at a time and check whether the count falls; it also takes about 30 questions but is harder to read.)

## Approach

1. Start `answer` at `0`.
2. For each `bit` from 0 to 29, build `mask = 1 << bit`.
3. Ask `commonSetBits(mask)`. A reply of `1` means `n` has this bit, so turn it on with `answer |= mask`.
4. After all 30 bits, `answer` equals `n`; return it.

## Example 1, step by step

The hidden `n = 31` is `11111` in binary. For `bit = 0` to `4`, the masks `1, 2, 4, 8, 16` each share their bit with `n`, so every reply is `1` and `answer` grows to `1, 3, 7, 15, 31`. For `bit = 5` to `29` the masks `32, 64, ...` share nothing with `n`, every reply is `0`, and `answer` stays `31`, which is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log M) questions, where M = 2^30: exactly 30 calls, one per bit.
- Space: O(1): just the running `answer`.

## Pitfalls

- Test the reply against `1` (or "greater than 0"), not against `mask`: `commonSetBits` returns a count, not the shared bits.
- Stay within 30 bits. `1 << 30` is already outside the allowed range of `num`, and `1 << 31` is negative in JavaScript.
- There is no input to read: `findNumber` gets no arguments, so everything must come from `commonSetBits`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `answer` | the bits of `n` confirmed so far |
| `bit` | the bit position being asked about |
| `mask` | a number whose only `1` bit is at position `bit` |

narration.2: Start with no bits known; every confirmed bit will be switched on here.
narration.3: The hidden number fits in 30 bits, so ask about each position 0 to 29 once.
narration.4: Build a number whose only 1 bit is at this position.
narration.5: A shared count of 1 means the hidden number has this bit set as well.
narration.6: Switch the confirmed bit on in the answer.
narration.9: All 30 bits are known, so the answer is the hidden number.
